title: Hegel

cards.h: The philosopher of the state and history
cards.b:
G.W.F. Hegel (1770-1831) built a huge system in which history, freedom and the state unfold through reason. Marx turned him upside down; liberals fear him. UPSC asks about his dialectic, civil society, the state, and the Marxist inversion.

His Philosophy of Right (1820) treats the family, civil society and the state as stages of ethical life. That idea is the core of his political theory.

History is the story of Spirit (Geist) coming to know itself as free. In Phenomenology of Spirit (1807) the master-slave dialectic shows that freedom grows from mutual recognition. In his words, 'The history of the world is none other than the progress of the consciousness of freedom.'

In Elements of the Philosophy of Right Hegel describes ethical life (Sittlichkeit) in three moments.

  • Family: unity by love.
  • Civil society: individuals in the market, with needs, classes and law. It creates wealth and also a poor 'rabble'.
  • State: the universal, where freedom becomes real.

For Hegel the state is 'the actuality of the ethical Idea' and the 'march of God in the world'. It does not mean that every state is divine. A rational state reconciles individual liberty and the community: citizens find freedom through its laws. He favoured a constitutional monarchy, a professional bureaucracy as the 'universal class', and estates for representation.

In Philosophy of History he sees freedom growing from one person free (Orient), some free (Greece and Rome), to all free (the Germanic Christian world). 'World-historical individuals' like Napoleon, driven by passion, serve Reason by a 'cunning of reason'. 'The owl of Minerva begins its flight only with the onset of dusk': philosophy understands an age only when it is ending.

For Hegel freedom is not doing as you please (that is arbitrary will). It is acting in line with reason inside institutions that you can recognise as your own. The family, the market and the state give a person roles that make real freedom possible. This is a classic example of what Berlin later called positive liberty. Compare Kant (moral autonomy) and Rousseau (self-given law). Hegel adds history and institutions to both.

• Marx, Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right (1843): Hegel's 'mystified' idealism; real basis is material. The state does not reconcile classes but serves the ruling class.
  • Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945): Hegel as a source of totalitarianism.
  • Eurocentric stages: he dismissed Africa and India as outside history.
  • Defenders: he is a theorist of modern freedom and institutions.

Young Hegelians and Marx took the dialectic and made it materialist. Kojeve read the master-slave dialectic, and Fukuyama's The End of History (1992) borrows it. Honneth and Taylor revived 'recognition'. T.H. Green and the British idealists used Hegel to argue for a positive state.

Karl Popper in The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945) blamed Hegel for paving the way to totalitarian thinking, a charge still argued about today.

In Philosophy of History Hegel treated India as a stagnant, dream-like civilisation without real history, a view later used to justify colonial rule. Indian thinkers such as Aurobindo and Radhakrishnan answered with their own accounts of spirit in history. Marx's use of the dialectic shaped Indian Marxists like M.N. Roy.

"Explain Hegel's dialectic and its use by Marx."
"Distinguish civil society and state in Hegel."
"Is Hegel a philosopher of freedom or of the authoritarian state?"

Structure: dialectic, Sittlichkeit, state, history, Marx's critique, Popper, legacy, India.

A good answer quotes the line 'the real is rational and the rational is real' from the preface to the Philosophy of Right, and then explains its limits.
